title: "Appendix A.0 The Dirac Delta Function"

> [!TLDR]
> The Dirac delta distribution selects values under integrals and represents a point charge density.

<!-- PDF page 380; printed page 372 -->

The Dirac delta function, $\delta(x)$, is an infinitely high, infinitesimally narrow spike at the origin, with area 1 (Fig. A.1). Specifically

$$
\delta(x)=\begin{cases}0,&\text{if }x\ne0\\\infty,&\text{if }x=0\end{cases}
\quad\text{and}\quad
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\delta(x)\,dx=1
\tag{A.1}
$$

Technically it's not a function at all, since its value is not finite at $x=0$. In the mathematical literature it is known as a *generalized function*, or *distribution*. It is, if you like, the *limit* of a sequence of functions, such as rectangles of height $n$ and width $1/n$, or isosceles triangles of height $n$ and base $2/n$ (Fig. A.2), or any other shape you might wish to use.

If $f(x)$ is some “ordinary” function (that is, *not* another delta function—in fact, just to be on the safe side let's say that $f(x)$ is *continuous*—then the *product* $f(x)\delta(x)$ is zero everywhere except at $x=0$. It follows that

$$
f(x)\delta(x)=f(0)\delta(x)
\tag{A.2}
$$

(This is the most important fact about the delta function, so make sure you understand why it is true. The point is that since the product is zero anyway except at $x=0$, we may as well replace $f(x)$ by the value it assumes at the origin.) In particular

$$
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(x)\delta(x)\,dx
=f(0)\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\delta(x)\,dx=f(0)
\tag{A.3}
$$

Under an integral, the delta function “picks out” the value of $f(x)$ at $x=0$. (Here and below, the integral need not run from $-\infty$ to $+\infty$; it is sufficient that the domain extend across the delta function, and $-\epsilon$ to $+\epsilon$ would do just as well.)

Of course, we can move the spike from $x=0$ to some other point, $x=a$:

$$
\delta(x-a)=\begin{cases}0,&\text{if }x\ne a\\\infty,&\text{if }x=a\end{cases}
\quad\text{and}\quad
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\delta(x-a)\,dx=1
\tag{A.4}
$$

**Fig. A.1** The Dirac delta function (you must imagine, however, that the curve is infinitely high and infinitesimally narrow).

(see Fig. A.3). Equation (A.2) generalizes to

$$
f(x)\delta(x-a)=f(a)\delta(x-a)
\tag{A.5}
$$

and equation (A.3) generalizes to

$$
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(x)\delta(x-a)\,dx=f(a)
\tag{A.6}
$$

Now, how would we interpret the expression $\delta(kx)$, if $k$ is some nonzero (real) number? Suppose we multiply by an “ordinary” function $f(x)$ and integrate:

$$
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(x)\delta(kx)\,dx
$$

We may change variables, letting $y\equiv kx$, so that $x=y/k$, and $dx=1/k\,dy$. If $k$ is *positive*, the integration still runs from $-\infty$ to $+\infty$, but if $k$ is *negative*, then $x=\infty$ implies $y=-\infty$, and *vice versa*, so the order of the limits is reversed. Restoring the “proper” order costs a minus sign. Thus

$$
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(x)\delta(kx)\,dx
=\pm\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(y/k)\delta(y)\frac{dy}{k}
=\pm\frac{1}{k}f(0)=\frac{1}{|k|}f(0)
\tag{A.7}
$$

(The lower signs apply when $k$ is negative, and we can account for this neatly by putting absolute value bars around the $k$, as indicated.) In this context, then, $\delta(kx)$ serves the same purpose as $(1/|k|)\delta(x)$:

$$
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(x)\delta(kx)\,dx
=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(x)\left[\frac{1}{|k|}\delta(x)\right]dx
\tag{A.8}
$$

**Fig. A.3** “Graph” of $\delta(x-a)$.

Because this holds for *any* $f(x)$, it follows that the delta function expressions are equal:[^ep-a-equality]

$$
\delta(kx)=\frac{1}{|k|}\delta(x)
\tag{A.9}
$$

What we have just analyzed is really a special case of the general form $\delta(g(x))$, where $g(x)$ is some function of $x$. $\delta(g(x))$ has spikes at the zeros, $x_1,x_2,x_3,\ldots$, of $g(x)$:

$$
g(x_i)=0\qquad(i=1,2,3,\ldots,n)
\tag{A.10}
$$

In the neighborhood of the $i$th zero, we may expand $g(x)$ as a Taylor series:

$$
g(x)=g(x_i)+(x-x_i)g'(x_i)+\tfrac12(x-x_i)^2g''(x_i)+\cdots
\cong(x-x_i)g'(x_i)
\tag{A.11}
$$

In view of equation (A.9), the spike at $x_i$ has the form

$$
\delta(g(x))=\frac{1}{|g'(x_i)|}\delta(x-x_i)
\qquad(x\cong x_i)
\tag{A.12}
$$

The factor $|g'(x_i)|^{-1}$ tells us the “strength” of the delta function at $x_i$. Putting this together with the spikes at the other zeros, we conclude

$$
\delta(g(x))=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{|g'(x_i)|}\delta(x-x_i)
\tag{A.13}
$$

Thus any expression of the form $\delta(g(x))$ can be reduced to a sum of simple delta functions.[^ep-a-exact]

## Example A.1

Simplify the expression $\delta(x^2+x-2)$.

*Solution.* Here $g(x)=x^2+x-2=(x-1)(x+2)$; there are two zeros, at $x_1=1$ and $x_2=-2$. Differentiating, $g'(x)=2x+1$, so $g'(x_1)=3$ and $g'(x_2)=-3$. Thus

$$
\delta(x^2+x-2)=\tfrac13\delta(x-1)+\tfrac13\delta(x+2)
$$

[^ep-a-equality]: You ought to ponder that last step for a moment. Ordinarily, the equality of two integrals certainly does *not* imply equality of the integrands. The crucial point here is that the integrals are equal for *any* $f(x)$. Suppose the delta function expressions $\delta(kx)$ and $(1/|k|)\delta(x)$ actually *differed*, say, in the neighborhood of the point $x=17$. Then I would pick a function $f(x)$ that was sharply peaked about $x=17$, and the integrals would not be equal. Since, on the contrary, the integrals *must* be equal, it follows that the delta function expressions are themselves equal. [Well, technically they might still differ at isolated points, provided these contribute nothing to the integral. But we can silence this objection by noting that both sides of equation (A.9) are clearly zero except at $x=0$.]

[^ep-a-exact]: Equation (A.13) is *exact*, notwithstanding the truncated Taylor series (A.11) I used in its derivation. At $x_i$, the “extra” terms are zero, since they contain powers of $(x-x_i)$.

<!-- PDF page 383; printed page 375 -->

It is an easy matter to generalize to three (or more) dimensions:

$$
\delta^3(\mechanical{\mathbf r})=\delta(\mechanical{x})\delta(\mechanical{y})\delta(\mechanical{z})
\tag{A.14}
$$

This three-dimensional delta function is zero everywhere except at the origin, where it blows up. The triple integral over $\delta^3(\mechanical{\mathbf r})$ is 1:

$$
\int\delta^3(\mechanical{\mathbf r})\,d^3\mechanical{\mathbf r}
=\int\delta(\mechanical{x})\delta(\mechanical{y})\delta(\mechanical{z})\,d\mechanical{x}\,d\mechanical{y}\,d\mechanical{z}=1
\tag{A.15}
$$

and

$$
\int f(\mechanical{\mathbf r})\delta^3(\mechanical{\mathbf r}-\mechanical{\mathbf r}_0)\,d^3\mechanical{\mathbf r}=f(\mechanical{\mathbf r}_0)
\tag{A.16}
$$

For example, the charge density (charge per unit volume) of a point charge $\electric{q}$ located at the point $\mechanical{\mathbf r}_0$ can be written

$$
\electric{\rho}(\mechanical{\mathbf r})=\electric{q}\,\delta^3(\mechanical{\mathbf r}-\mechanical{\mathbf r}_0)
$$

## Problems

### Problem A.1

(a) $\int_0^3(2x^2+7x+3)\delta(x-1)\,dx=?$

(b) $\int_0^3\ln(1+x)\delta(\pi-x)\,dx=?$

### Problem A.2

Use equation (A.13) to simplify the expression $\delta(\sqrt{x^2+1}-x-1)$.

### Problem A.3

Use equation (A.13) to simplify the expression $\delta(\sin x)$. Sketch this function.

### Problem A.4

Let $f(y)=\int_0^2\delta(y-x(2-x))\,dx$. Find $f(y)$, and plot it from $y=-2$ to $y=+2$.

### Problem A.5

$\int_{-1}^5 x^4\left[\frac{d^2}{dx^2}\delta(x-3)\right]dx=?$ [*Hint:* Integrate by parts.]

### Problem A.6

Evaluate $\int\mechanical{\mathbf r}\cdot(\mechanical{\mathbf a}-\mechanical{\mathbf r})\delta^3(\mechanical{\mathbf r}-\mechanical{\mathbf b})\,d^3\mechanical{\mathbf r}$, if $\mechanical{\mathbf a}=(1,2,3)$, $\mechanical{\mathbf b}=(3,2,1)$, and the integration is over a sphere of radius 1.5 centered at $(2,2,2)$.

## Physical quantities

| Symbol | Unit | Quantity | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\mechanical{\mathbf r},\mechanical{x},\mechanical{y},\mechanical{z}$ | $\unit{\mathrm{cm}}$ | Position | The point and its Cartesian coordinates in three-dimensional space. |
| $\mechanical{\mathbf r}_0$ | $\unit{\mathrm{cm}}$ | Charge position | The position of the point charge. |
| $\electric{q}$ | $\unit{\mathrm{statC}}$ | Electric charge | The charge at the specified position. |
| $\electric{\rho}$ | $\unit{\mathrm{statC/cm^3}}$ | Charge density | The electric charge per unit volume. |
| $\mechanical{\mathbf a},\mechanical{\mathbf b}$ | $\unit{\mathrm{cm}}$ | Fixed positions | The two position vectors in Problem A.6. |
